Compression Bounds

Lesson text (draft) · Teacher's sheet

Four messages out of ten thousand

The auditor is back. Compliance sent her at the end of lesson 17, with the rule that every filtering decision must be explainable, and in lesson 18 she read your decision trees. She has been reading your filters ever since. This time she has the tightest-box filter on her desk, the one from lesson 8. It looks at two scores of a message, x1x_1x1​, the share of capital letters in the subject, and x2x_2x2​, the share of the body taken up by links, and it calls a message junk when both scores fall inside a box: one interval for capitals, one for links. The learner draws the tightest such box around the junk examples. This quarter it was trained on m=10,000m = 10{,}000m=10,000 messages that your users labelled.

She did something nobody on the team had thought of. She deleted the training messages one at a time and retrained after each deletion, to see which ones mattered. Almost none did. In the end she kept exactly four messages: the junk message with the fewest capitals, the one with the most capitals, the one with the fewest links and the one with the most links. She retrained on those four alone, and out came the same box, to the last decimal.

“So your filter is really four messages,” she says. “The other 9,996 played no part in it. Doesn’t that mean they are an exam it never saw? And if it passes that exam, is that a certificate?”

It is a sharp question, and the team has no tool that answers it. Lesson 6 certifies the box through its VC dimension, which talks about the class of all boxes and says nothing about how the learner used its examples. Lesson 13 certifies stable learners. Nothing you own turns “this hypothesis can be rebuilt from a few of its examples” into a statement about its true risk. This lesson builds that tool. It is called a compression bound, and the auditor’s instinct turns out to be very nearly right, with one twist that costs a logarithm.

Here is her experiment in Python. The messages are drawn at random, junk exactly when both scores fall inside the true box [0.3,0.8]×[0.2,0.6][0.3, 0.8] \times [0.2, 0.6][0.3,0.8]×[0.2,0.6] (capitals between 0.3 and 0.8 and links between 0.2 and 0.6, the ×\times× pairing one interval per score as in lesson 8), the learner draws the tightest box around the junk, and then we keep only four positions and rebuild:

import random
rng = random.Random(30)
a, b = (0.3, 0.2), (0.8, 0.6)
def inside(x, lo, hi):
    return all(l <= v <= u for v, l, u in zip(x, lo, hi))
xs = [(rng.random(), rng.random()) for _ in range(10_000)]
S = [(x, int(inside(x, a, b))) for x in xs]
P = [i for i, (x, y) in enumerate(S, 1) if y == 1]
I = [f(P, key=lambda i: S[i - 1][0][j]) for j in (0, 1)
     for f in (min, max)]
kept = [S[i - 1][0] for i in I]
lo = [min(x[j] for x in kept) for j in (0, 1)]
hi = [max(x[j] for x in kept) for j in (0, 1)]
errs = sum(int(inside(x, lo, hi)) != y for x, y in S)
print(len(S), len(P), I, errs)

It prints 10000 2010 [1003, 4750, 3348, 5037] 0: ten thousand messages, 2,010 of them junk, the four kept positions, and a rebuilt box that makes no mistake on any of the ten thousand.

Rebuilding a box, example by example

Let’s slow down and do the same thing by hand on a sequence small enough to hold in your head. These are the eight examples from lesson 8, with label 1 for junk and 0 for keep:

icapitals x1x_1x1​links x2x_2x2​label
10.350.25junk
20.600.50junk
30.500.30junk
40.750.40junk
50.100.30keep
60.900.50keep
70.500.80keep
80.400.10keep

Recall how lesson 8 drew the tightest box: for each score, the interval runs from the smallest to the largest value that score takes among the junk examples. That gave [0.35,0.75]×[0.25,0.5][0.35, 0.75] \times [0.25, 0.5][0.35,0.75]×[0.25,0.5]. Now ask a different question: which examples actually set those four numbers? Before you read on, find them in the table.

Each end of each interval is set by one junk example, so there are four slots to fill.

slotwhat it asksjunk valueswinner
1fewest capitals0.35, 0.60, 0.50, 0.75example 1 (0.35)
2most capitals0.35, 0.60, 0.50, 0.75example 4 (0.75)
3fewest links0.25, 0.50, 0.30, 0.40example 1 (0.25)
4most links0.25, 0.50, 0.30, 0.40example 2 (0.50)

So the box is pinned by the list of positions (1,4,1,2)(1, 4, 1, 2)(1,4,1,2). Notice that example 1 fills two slots, because it has both the fewest capitals and the fewest links. The list has four entries but only three different examples. Hold on to that; it matters for the theory.

Now rebuild: hand the learner only the examples at those positions, (z1,z4,z1,z2)(z_1, z_4, z_1, z_2)(z1​,z4​,z1​,z2​), where ziz_izi​ is the iii-th example, message and label together, and let it draw the tightest box around their junk. The smallest capitals among them is 0.35 and the largest 0.75; the smallest links 0.25 and the largest 0.5. Same box. And since it is the same box, it makes the same zero mistakes on all eight examples. The four keep messages, 5 to 8, were never consulted at all.

S = [((0.35, 0.25), 1), ((0.6, 0.5), 1), ((0.5, 0.3), 1),
     ((0.75, 0.4), 1), ((0.1, 0.3), 0), ((0.9, 0.5), 0),
     ((0.5, 0.8), 0), ((0.4, 0.1), 0)]
P = [i for i, (x, y) in enumerate(S, 1) if y == 1]
I = [f(P, key=lambda i: S[i - 1][0][j]) for j in (0, 1)
     for f in (min, max)]
print(I, len(set(I)))

It prints [1, 4, 1, 2] 3: four slots, three distinct examples.

There are two halves to what just happened, and they deserve names. The first half looked at the whole training sequence and chose a short list of positions. The second half looked only at the examples at those positions and built a hypothesis. A pair like that, where the hypothesis built from the short list is consistent with the whole sequence, is a compression scheme, and the length of the list is its size. For boxes in two scores the size is 4. We will make all of this precise soon; first, play with it.

An exam the box never saw

The auditor’s intuition goes like this. Suppose you build a hypothesis from a handful of examples, and then grade it on a completely separate batch it never touched. The grade on that separate batch is an honest estimate of the true risk, for exactly the reason lesson 11 gave for its validation set: the batch is a fresh sample from D\mathcal DD, the distribution the mail comes from, and the hypothesis was fixed before the batch was drawn.

Let’s state that protocol carefully, because the whole lesson leans on it. First draw kkk examples, call this sequence TTT, and build a hypothesis hTh_ThT​ from it, by any method you like. Then draw a fresh sequence of further examples, call it VVV (for “validation”), and compute the empirical risk of hTh_ThT​ on VVV. Recall that the empirical risk LV(h)L_V(h)LV​(h) is the fraction of the examples in VVV that hhh gets wrong, and the true risk LD(h)L_{\mathcal D}(h)LD​(h) is the probability that hhh mislabels a fresh message drawn from the distribution D\mathcal DD. The question is how far apart LV(hT)L_V(h_T)LV​(hT​) and LD(hT)L_{\mathcal D}(h_T)LD​(hT​) can be.

You already own one answer. Hoeffding’s inequality from lesson 4 says that the average of nnn independent quantities in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] lies within log⁡(2/δ)/(2n)\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}log(2/δ)/(2n)​ of its mean, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ. (Here log⁡\loglog is the natural logarithm, δ\deltaδ is the confidence parameter, the chance we allow ourselves to be wrong, and nnn is the number of examples in VVV.) With n=1,000n = 1{,}000n=1,000 and δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05 that slack is about 0.043.

Now look at that number next to a good filter. If the true risk is 0.02, a slack of 0.043 is more than twice the thing you are measuring. Hoeffding is wasteful here, and it is wasteful for a reason you can see. It has to cover the worst case, a quantity that is 0 half the time and 1 half the time, which swings as much as any quantity in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] can. A mistake indicator with rate 0.02 is almost always 0. Its swings are tiny. The count of mistakes in 1,000 messages has mean 20 and, as you will compute in a moment, a spread of only about 4.4 either way. We want a tool that notices how small the swings are.

Bernstein’s inequality

The tool is called Bernstein’s inequality, and the idea it carries is this: a sum of small, quiet quantities stays close to its mean, and how close depends on how much the quantities actually vary, not on the worst they could do.

To measure “how much a quantity varies” we use its variance. For a random number ZZZ with mean 0, the variance is E[Z2]\mathbb E[Z^2]E[Z2], the average squared distance from the mean. (E\mathbb EE is the expectation: the average value, weighted by probability.) Take a single message and let ZZZ be “1 if the filter errs on it, else 0”, minus the error rate 0.02, so that its mean is 0. It equals 0.980.980.98 with probability 0.02 and −0.02-0.02−0.02 with probability 0.98, so

E[Z2]=0.02⋅0.982+0.98⋅0.022=0.02⋅0.98=0.0196.\mathbb E[Z^2] = 0.02 \cdot 0.98^2 + 0.98 \cdot 0.02^2 = 0.02 \cdot 0.98 = 0.0196.E[Z2]=0.02⋅0.982+0.98⋅0.022=0.02⋅0.98=0.0196.

Over 1,000 independent messages the variances add, to 19.619.619.6, and the typical spread of the mistake count is the square root, 19.6≈4.4\sqrt{19.6} \approx 4.419.6​≈4.4. Compare the worst-case quantity Hoeffding prepares for: variance 1/41/41/4 per message, 250 in total, spread about 16. Bernstein lets us use the 19.6.

[diagram:variance: built on the lesson page]

Bernstein’s inequality. Let Z1,…,ZmZ_1, \dots, Z_mZ1​,…,Zm​ be independent and identically distributed random variables with mean zero, and suppose ∣Zi∣<M|Z_i| < M∣Zi​∣<M with probability 1 for every iii. Then for every t>0t > 0t>0,

P[∑i=1mZi>t]≤exp⁡(−t2/2∑j=1mE[Zj2]+Mt/3).\mathbb P\left[ \sum_{i=1}^m Z_i > t \right] \le \exp\left( - \frac{t^2 / 2}{\sum_{j=1}^m \mathbb E[Z_j^2] + M t / 3} \right).P[i=1∑m​Zi​>t]≤exp(−∑j=1m​E[Zj2​]+Mt/3t2/2​).

Read it from the inside out.

  • ZiZ_iZi​ is the iii-th random quantity, in our story “mistake on message iii, minus the error rate”. Independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) means each is drawn the same way and none influences another.
  • ∣Zi∣<M|Z_i| < M∣Zi​∣<M says no single quantity can be larger than MMM in size; ∣⋅∣|\cdot|∣⋅∣ is the absolute value here. For mistake indicators minus their mean, M=1M = 1M=1 works.
  • ∑i=1mZi\sum_{i=1}^m Z_i∑i=1m​Zi​ adds the mmm quantities. In the story it is “the number of mistakes, minus the expected number”.
  • ttt is a threshold, how far above its mean we fear the sum might land.
  • P[… ]\mathbb P[\dots]P[…] is the probability of the event inside the brackets: the sum exceeds its mean by more than ttt.
  • In the denominator, ∑jE[Zj2]\sum_j \mathbb E[Z_j^2]∑j​E[Zj2​] is the total variance, the 19.6 above, and Mt/3Mt/3Mt/3 is a correction for the rare large jump.
  • exp⁡(⋅)\exp(\cdot)exp(⋅) is eee raised to the given power, so a large fraction inside means a tiny probability.

In plain words: the chance that a sum of bounded, mean-zero quantities overshoots by ttt shrinks like e−t2/(2⋅variance)e^{-t^2/(2 \cdot \text{variance})}e−t2/(2⋅variance) as long as ttt is small next to the variance divided by MMM, and like e−3t/(2M)e^{-3t/(2M)}e−3t/(2M) beyond that. Push the story through it. With 1,000 messages at error rate 0.02, ask for the chance of more than 15 extra mistakes, that is 36 or more in all: t=15t = 15t=15, total variance 19.6, M=1M = 1M=1, so the exponent is −112.5/(19.6+5)≈−4.57-112.5 / (19.6 + 5) \approx -4.57−112.5/(19.6+5)≈−4.57 and the bound is about 0.0103. Hoeffding’s version of the same question, e−2t2/me^{-2t^2/m}e−2t2/m, gives 0.64, which is almost useless. The exact binomial probability is smaller still.

from math import comb, exp
m, L_D, t = 1000, 0.02, 15
var_sum = m * L_D * (1 - L_D)
bernstein = exp(-(t ** 2 / 2) / (var_sum + t / 3))
hoeffding = exp(-2 * t ** 2 / m)
exact = sum(comb(m, j) * L_D ** j * (1 - L_D) ** (m - j)
            for j in range(m + 1) if j - m * L_D > t)
print(round(var_sum, 1), round(bernstein, 4))
print(round(hoeffding, 4), round(exact, 4))

It prints 19.6 0.0103 and then 0.6376 0.0007. In the code, var_sum is ∑jE[Zj2]\sum_j \mathbb E[Z_j^2]∑j​E[Zj2​], bernstein is the right-hand side of the inequality term by term, and exact adds up the binomial probabilities of every mistake count more than 15 above 20. Bernstein is within a factor of fifteen of the truth; Hoeffding is off by a factor of nine hundred.

We will use Bernstein’s inequality as a tool, without proof. Its proof follows the same path as Hoeffding’s (bound the exponential moment E[eλZ]\mathbb E[e^{\lambda Z}]E[eλZ], then apply Markov’s inequality), but it keeps track of the variance along the way.

One fixed hypothesis, both directions

Now we turn Bernstein into a statement about risks. Fix one hypothesis hhh before seeing any data. Its empirical risk on a random sample is an average of mistake indicators, so it should be close to its true risk, and when the true risk is small the slack should be small too. There are two directions to say this in: the training error is probably not much above the true risk, and the true risk is probably not much above the training error. The second is the one we need, because in practice we can see LS(h)L_S(h)LS​(h) and want to bound LD(h)L_{\mathcal D}(h)LD​(h).

We state it for any loss with values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. Recall that H\mathcal HH is the hypothesis class, Z\mathcal ZZ the set of all possible examples, and that a loss function ℓ(h,z)\ell(h, z)ℓ(h,z) scores hypothesis hhh on example zzz; for the 0-1 loss it is 1 on a mistake and 0 otherwise, and then LS(h)=1m∑iℓ(h,zi)L_S(h) = \frac1m \sum_i \ell(h, z_i)LS​(h)=m1​∑i​ℓ(h,zi​) and LD(h)=Ez∼D[ℓ(h,z)]L_{\mathcal D}(h) = \mathbb E_{z \sim \mathcal D}[\ell(h, z)]LD​(h)=Ez∼D​[ℓ(h,z)], where z∼Dz \sim \mathcal Dz∼D reads “zzz is drawn from D\mathcal DD”.

Lemma (a fixed hypothesis, measured by Bernstein). Let ℓ:H×Z→[0,1]\ell: \mathcal H \times \mathcal Z \to [0, 1]ℓ:H×Z→[0,1] be a loss function, D\mathcal DD any distribution over examples, and hhh a fixed hypothesis. Then for every δ∈(0,1)\delta \in (0, 1)δ∈(0,1),

(1)PS∼Dm[LS(h)≥LD(h)+2LD(h)log⁡(1/δ)m+2log⁡(1/δ)3m]≤δ,\text{(1)} \quad \mathbb P_{S \sim \mathcal D^m}\left[ L_S(h) \ge L_{\mathcal D}(h) + \sqrt{\frac{2 L_{\mathcal D}(h) \log(1/\delta)}{m}} + \frac{2 \log(1/\delta)}{3m} \right] \le \delta,(1)PS∼Dm​[LS​(h)≥LD​(h)+m2LD​(h)log(1/δ)​​+3m2log(1/δ)​]≤δ,
(2)PS∼Dm[LD(h)≥LS(h)+2LS(h)log⁡(1/δ)m+4log⁡(1/δ)m]≤δ.\text{(2)} \quad \mathbb P_{S \sim \mathcal D^m}\left[ L_{\mathcal D}(h) \ge L_S(h) + \sqrt{\frac{2 L_S(h) \log(1/\delta)}{m}} + \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{m} \right] \le \delta.(2)PS∼Dm​[LD​(h)≥LS​(h)+m2LS​(h)log(1/δ)​​+m4log(1/δ)​]≤δ.

Read them from the inside out.

  • S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm under the P\mathbb PP says the probability is over a random training sequence of mmm examples drawn i.i.d. from D\mathcal DD.
  • log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ) is the price of confidence: at δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05 it is about 3.0.
  • The square-root term is the variance-sensitive part. It has the risk itself under the root, so it vanishes when the risk is zero.
  • The last term, log⁡(1/δ)/m\log(1/\delta)/mlog(1/δ)/m times a constant, is the price of rare large jumps. It shrinks like 1/m1/m1/m, much faster than Hoeffding’s 1/m1/\sqrt m1/m​.
  • Part (1) has the true risk inside the root; part (2) has the empirical risk, which you can actually compute.

In plain words, part (2): with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, the true risk is at most the training error, plus a square root that scales with the training error, plus 4log⁡(1/δ)/m4\log(1/\delta)/m4log(1/δ)/m. For a hypothesis with true risk 0.02 and m=1,000m = 1{,}000m=1,000, δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05: if it shows the training error 0.02, the bound allows a true risk up to 0.02+2⋅0.02⋅3.0/1000+4⋅3.0/1000≈0.02+0.011+0.0120.02 + \sqrt{2 \cdot 0.02 \cdot 3.0/1000} + 4 \cdot 3.0/1000 \approx 0.02 + 0.011 + 0.0120.02+2⋅0.02⋅3.0/1000​+4⋅3.0/1000≈0.02+0.011+0.012, a slack of 0.023 against Hoeffding’s 0.043.

The simulation below draws 20,000 training sequences for a hypothesis with true risk 0.02, and counts how often each bad event of the lemma happens. The lemma promises at most 5% each.

import random
from math import log, sqrt
rng, m, delta, L_D = random.Random(1), 1000, 0.05, 0.02
L = log(1 / delta)
bad1 = bad2 = 0
for _ in range(20_000):
    L_S = sum(rng.random() < L_D for _ in range(m)) / m
    bad1 += L_S >= L_D + sqrt(2 * L_D * L / m) + 2 * L / (3 * m)
    bad2 += L_D >= L_S + sqrt(2 * L_S * L / m) + 4 * L / m
print(round(bad1 / 20_000, 4), round(bad2 / 20_000, 4))
print(round(sqrt(2 * 0.02 * L / m) + 4 * L / m, 4),
      round(sqrt(log(2 / delta) / (2 * m)), 4))

It prints 0.0037 0.0 and 0.0229 0.0429, the last two being the Bernstein slack of the worked example and Hoeffding’s slack log⁡(2/δ)/(2n)\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2n)}log(2/δ)/(2n)​ from the previous section. Each line of the loop is one of the two events, symbol for symbol. Both happen far less often than 5%: the constants are safe, not tight.

Proof of (1). Define αi=ℓ(h,zi)−LD(h)\alpha_i = \ell(h, z_i) - L_{\mathcal D}(h)αi​=ℓ(h,zi​)−LD​(h) for i∈[m]i \in [m]i∈[m], where [m][m][m] is the set of positions {1,…,m}\{1, \dots, m\}{1,…,m}. Each αi\alpha_iαi​ is a function of ziz_izi​ alone, and the ziz_izi​ are i.i.d., so the αi\alpha_iαi​ are i.i.d. too. Their mean is E[ℓ(h,zi)]−LD(h)=0\mathbb E[\ell(h, z_i)] - L_{\mathcal D}(h) = 0E[ℓ(h,zi​)]−LD​(h)=0, by the definition of the true risk.

Next, the variance. Expanding the square and using linearity of expectation,

E[αi2]=E[ℓ(h,zi)2]−2LD(h) E[ℓ(h,zi)]+LD(h)2=E[ℓ(h,zi)2]−LD(h)2≤E[ℓ(h,zi)2]≤LD(h).\mathbb E[\alpha_i^2] = \mathbb E[\ell(h, z_i)^2] - 2 L_{\mathcal D}(h)\, \mathbb E[\ell(h, z_i)] + L_{\mathcal D}(h)^2 = \mathbb E[\ell(h, z_i)^2] - L_{\mathcal D}(h)^2 \le \mathbb E[\ell(h, z_i)^2] \le L_{\mathcal D}(h).E[αi2​]=E[ℓ(h,zi​)2]−2LD​(h)E[ℓ(h,zi​)]+LD​(h)2=E[ℓ(h,zi​)2]−LD​(h)2≤E[ℓ(h,zi​)2]≤LD​(h).

The middle equality substitutes E[ℓ(h,zi)]=LD(h)\mathbb E[\ell(h, z_i)] = L_{\mathcal D}(h)E[ℓ(h,zi​)]=LD​(h). The first inequality drops a square, which is never negative. The last uses ℓ∈[0,1]\ell \in [0, 1]ℓ∈[0,1]: a number between 0 and 1 is at least its own square, so ℓ2≤ℓ\ell^2 \le \ellℓ2≤ℓ, and the expectation of ℓ\ellℓ is LD(h)L_{\mathcal D}(h)LD​(h). For a mistake indicator this is the 0.0196 ≤\le≤ 0.02 of the previous section.

Also ∣αi∣≤1|\alpha_i| \le 1∣αi​∣≤1, since both ℓ\ellℓ and LD(h)L_{\mathcal D}(h)LD​(h) lie in [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. So ∣αi∣<M|\alpha_i| < M∣αi​∣<M for every M>1M > 1M>1, and Bernstein applies for each such MMM. The probability on the left does not depend on MMM, so it is at most the smallest of these bounds, and letting MMM shrink to 1 gives the bound with M=1M = 1M=1. where the inequality is a+b≤a+b\sqrt{a + b} \le \sqrt a + \sqrt ba+b​≤a​+b​ (square both sides: a+b≤a+b+2aba + b \le a + b + 2\sqrt{ab}a+b≤a+b+2ab​). Call the right side t′t't′.

That proves (1).

Proof of (2). Apply Bernstein to −α1,…,−αm-\alpha_1, \dots, -\alpha_m−α1​,…,−αm​ instead. They are still i.i.d., with mean zero, the same variances and ∣−αi∣≤1|-\alpha_i| \le 1∣−αi​∣≤1, so with the same ttt, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ we have ∑i(−αi)≤t\sum_i (-\alpha_i) \le t∑i​(−αi​)≤t. Dividing by mmm and using the bound on ttt,

LD(h)−LS(h)≤a+b LD(h),a=2log⁡(1/δ)3m,b=2log⁡(1/δ)m.L_{\mathcal D}(h) - L_S(h) \le a + \sqrt{b\, L_{\mathcal D}(h)}, \qquad a = \frac{2\log(1/\delta)}{3m}, \quad b = \frac{2 \log(1/\delta)}{m}.LD​(h)−LS​(h)≤a+bLD​(h)​,a=3m2log(1/δ)​,b=m2log(1/δ)​.

This bounds the true risk by itself, under a square root. To free it, write x=LD(h)x = \sqrt{L_{\mathcal D}(h)}x=LD​(h)​ and c=LS(h)+ac = L_S(h) + ac=LS​(h)+a. The inequality reads x2−b x−c≤0x^2 - \sqrt b\, x - c \le 0x2−b​x−c≤0. A quadratic with positive leading coefficient is non-positive only between its roots, so xxx is at most the larger root:

x≤b+b+4c2.x \le \frac{\sqrt b + \sqrt{b + 4c}}{2}.x≤2b​+b+4c​​.

Squaring,

LD(h)=x2≤2b+4c+2b2+4bc4≤2b+4c+2(b+2bc)4=b+c+bc,L_{\mathcal D}(h) = x^2 \le \frac{2b + 4c + 2\sqrt{b^2 + 4bc}}{4} \le \frac{2b + 4c + 2(b + 2\sqrt{bc})}{4} = b + c + \sqrt{bc},LD​(h)=x2≤42b+4c+2b2+4bc​​≤42b+4c+2(b+2bc​)​=b+c+bc​,

where the middle step uses b2+4bc≤b+2bc\sqrt{b^2 + 4bc} \le b + 2\sqrt{bc}b2+4bc​≤b+2bc​ (square the right side: b2+4bbc+4bcb^2 + 4b\sqrt{bc} + 4bcb2+4bbc​+4bc, which is larger). Substitute c=LS(h)+ac = L_S(h) + ac=LS​(h)+a and split the root with bLS+ab≤bLS+ab\sqrt{bL_S + ab} \le \sqrt{bL_S} + \sqrt{ab}bLS​+ab​≤bLS​​+ab​:

LD(h)≤LS(h)+b LS(h)+(a+b+ab).L_{\mathcal D}(h) \le L_S(h) + \sqrt{b\, L_S(h)} + \left(a + b + \sqrt{ab}\right).LD​(h)≤LS​(h)+bLS​(h)​+(a+b+ab​).

Finally, the constants. With λ=log⁡(1/δ)/m\lambda = \log(1/\delta)/mλ=log(1/δ)/m we have a=23λa = \frac23\lambdaa=32​λ, b=2λb = 2\lambdab=2λ and ab=23λ\sqrt{ab} = \frac{2}{\sqrt3}\lambdaab​=3​2​λ, so a+b+ab=(23+2+23)λ≈3.82 λ<4λa + b + \sqrt{ab} = \left(\frac23 + 2 + \frac{2}{\sqrt 3}\right)\lambda \approx 3.82\,\lambda < 4\lambdaa+b+ab​=(32​+2+3​2​)λ≈3.82λ<4λ. And bLS(h)=2LS(h)log⁡(1/δ)/m\sqrt{b L_S(h)} = \sqrt{2 L_S(h)\log(1/\delta)/m}bLS​(h)​=2LS​(h)log(1/δ)/m​. So with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, the true risk is strictly less than the right side of (2), which means the bad event of (2) has probability at most δ\deltaδ. ■\blacksquare■

The constant is worth checking by machine, together with the whole chain of algebra. The snippet computes (a+b+ab)/λ(a + b + \sqrt{ab})/\lambda(a+b+ab​)/λ, then throws 100,000 random pairs (LS,LD)(L_S, L_{\mathcal D})(LS​,LD​) at the starting inequality and records the worst value of (LD−LS−bLS)/λ\left(L_{\mathcal D} - L_S - \sqrt{bL_S}\right)/\lambda(LD​−LS​−bLS​​)/λ among the pairs that satisfy it. The proof says that worst value never reaches 3.82.

import random
from math import log, sqrt
m, L = 1000, log(1 / 0.05)
a, b = 2 * L / (3 * m), 2 * L / m
print(round((a + b + sqrt(a * b)) / (L / m), 3))
rng, worst = random.Random(5), 0.0
for _ in range(100_000):
    L_S, L_D = rng.random(), rng.random()
    if L_D - L_S <= a + sqrt(b * L_D):
        gap = L_D - L_S - sqrt(b * L_S)
        worst = max(worst, gap / (L / m))
print(round(worst, 3))

It prints 3.821 and 2.074.

The hold-out lemma

Back to the protocol: build hTh_ThT​ from kkk examples, then grade it on a fresh, independent sequence VVV. Part (2) of the lemma was about a hypothesis fixed in advance. Here hTh_ThT​ is random, since it depends on TTT, but it is fixed before VVV is drawn, and that is all we need.

Lemma (hold-out). Let the loss take values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. Let TTT be a sequence of kkk examples, hTh_ThT​ any hypothesis computed from TTT, and VVV a sequence of examples drawn i.i.d. from D\mathcal DD, independently of TTT. Then

P[LD(hT)−LV(hT)≥2LV(hT)log⁡(1/δ)∣V∣+4log⁡(1/δ)∣V∣]≤δ.\mathbb P\left[ L_{\mathcal D}(h_T) - L_V(h_T) \ge \sqrt{\frac{2 L_V(h_T) \log(1/\delta)}{|V|}} + \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{|V|} \right] \le \delta.P[LD​(hT​)−LV​(hT​)≥∣V∣2LV​(hT​)log(1/δ)​​+∣V∣4log(1/δ)​]≤δ.

Here ∣V∣|V|∣V∣ is the number of examples in VVV, LV(hT)L_V(h_T)LV​(hT​) is the fraction of them that hTh_ThT​ gets wrong, and the probability is over both TTT and VVV. In plain words: a hypothesis graded on examples it never saw has a true risk at most its grade plus a Bernstein slack sized by that grade and by the number of examples graded. With ∣V∣=9,996|V| = 9{,}996∣V∣=9,996, a grade of 0 and δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05, the slack is 4⋅3.0/9,996≈0.00124 \cdot 3.0 / 9{,}996 \approx 0.00124⋅3.0/9,996≈0.0012: if the auditor had chosen the four messages before seeing any data, the box would be certified to within about a tenth of a percent.

Proof. Condition on TTT. Once TTT is known, hTh_ThT​ is one fixed hypothesis. Because VVV is independent of TTT, knowing TTT does not change how VVV is distributed: given TTT, VVV is still ∣V∣|V|∣V∣ examples drawn i.i.d. from D\mathcal DD. So part (2) of the previous lemma applies, with VVV in the role of SSS and ∣V∣|V|∣V∣ in the role of mmm, and the conditional probability of the bad event, given TTT, is at most δ\deltaδ. This holds for every possible value of TTT. The unconditional probability is the average of the conditional ones over TTT (the law of total probability), and an average of numbers that are each at most δ\deltaδ is at most δ\deltaδ. ■\blacksquare■

Here is the protocol as an experiment. Each round draws k=4k = 4k=4 fresh messages, builds the tightest box around their junk (or the empty box, which says keep everywhere, if none of the four is junk), then grades it on 2,000 fresh messages. Because the box built from junk always sits inside the true box, its true risk is exactly the area of the true box, 0.2, minus the area of the built box. The lemma promises the bad event in at most 5% of rounds.

import random
from math import log, sqrt
rng, k, n, delta = random.Random(15), 4, 2000, 0.05
a, b = (0.3, 0.2), (0.8, 0.6)
def inside(x, lo, hi):
    return all(lo[j] <= x[j] <= hi[j] for j in (0, 1))
draw = lambda: (rng.random(), rng.random())
bad = 0
for _ in range(2000):
    P = [x for x in (draw() for _ in range(k)) if inside(x, a, b)]
    lo = [min((x[j] for x in P), default=1) for j in (0, 1)]
    hi = [max((x[j] for x in P), default=0) for j in (0, 1)]
    L_D = 0.2 - max(0, hi[0] - lo[0]) * max(0, hi[1] - lo[1])
    V = [draw() for _ in range(n)]
    L_V = sum(inside(x, a, b) != inside(x, lo, hi) for x in V) / n
    c = log(1 / delta) / n
    bad += L_D - L_V >= sqrt(2 * L_V * c) + 4 * c
print(bad / 2000)

It prints 0.0005: one bad round in two thousand.

The catch: the four were chosen by looking

So far so good. But reread the auditor’s claim. Her four messages were not chosen in advance. They were chosen after looking at all ten thousand: they are the extremes, and you only know which messages are extreme once you have seen them all. The remaining 9,996 are not “an exam drawn after the hypothesis was fixed”. They are “whatever was left over after a choice that looked at everything”.

Does that matter? It can. Imagine a sneakier learner that, for every possible choice of four positions, builds a box, grades it on the other 9,996, and returns whichever box got the best grade. Each individual grade is honest, but the best of many honest grades is biased: it is the one that got lucky. This is the same trap as lesson 2’s overfitting and lesson 11’s reused validation set. Picking the winner after looking at the scores spoils the scores.

There is a way out, and it is the oldest trick in the course. First notice that the hold-out argument never cared how TTT was drawn, only that VVV was independent of it. So consider this version of the protocol. Before seeing any data, agree on a list of kkk positions I=(i1,…,ik)I = (i_1, \dots, i_k)I=(i1​,…,ik​), each between 1 and mmm, repeats allowed. Then draw S=(z1,…,zm)S = (z_1, \dots, z_m)S=(z1​,…,zm​), set T=(zi1,…,zik)T = (z_{i_1}, \dots, z_{i_k})T=(zi1​​,…,zik​​), and let VVV be the examples at the other positions. Since the zzz’s are independent, the examples at the chosen positions are independent of the examples at the rest, so the hold-out lemma holds for this fixed III.

The learner, however, does not use a fixed III. It picks one after looking. So we make the hold-out lemma hold for every III at once, with the union bound from lesson 2: the probability that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their probabilities. How many lists of kkk positions are there? Each of the kkk entries is one of mmm positions, so mkm^kmk. For the auditor’s box that is 10,0004=101610{,}000^4 = 10^{16}10,0004=1016, an absurd number of events. But in the bound it will only appear through its logarithm, and log⁡1016=4log⁡10,000≈36.8\log 10^{16} = 4 \log 10{,}000 \approx 36.8log1016=4log10,000≈36.8. That is the price of choosing by looking: about klog⁡mk \log mklogm where the fixed protocol paid nothing.

from math import log
m, k = 10_000, 4
print(m ** k, round(k * log(m), 2))

It prints 10000000000000000 36.84.

[diagram:union-over-indices: built on the lesson page]

The compression bound

We are ready for the main result. It is stated for any learner whose output can be rebuilt from kkk of its own examples by a fixed reconstruction function BBB: a function that takes a sequence of kkk examples and returns a hypothesis from H\mathcal HH. The learner AAA may choose which kkk positions to use after looking at all of SSS; the theorem only asks that its output is BBB applied to the examples at some kkk positions. For a list of positions I=(i1,…,ik)I = (i_1, \dots, i_k)I=(i1​,…,ik​) we write SI=(zi1,…,zik)S_I = (z_{i_1}, \dots, z_{i_k})SI​=(zi1​​,…,zik​​) for the examples at those positions, and the set of all such lists is written [m]k[m]^k[m]k, “lists of length kkk with entries from [m][m][m]”.

Theorem (the compression bound). Let kkk be a positive integer, B:Zk→HB: \mathcal Z^k \to \mathcal HB:Zk→H a function from sequences of kkk examples to hypotheses, and m≥2km \ge 2km≥2k. Let the loss take values in [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. Let AAA be a learner that, on every training sequence SSS of mmm examples, returns A(S)=B(SI)A(S) = B(S_I)A(S)=B(SI​) for some I=(i1,…,ik)∈[m]kI = (i_1, \dots, i_k) \in [m]^kI=(i1​,…,ik​)∈[m]k, and let VVV be the examples of SSS whose positions are not in III. Then for every δ∈(0,1)\delta \in (0,1)δ∈(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm,

LD(A(S))≤LV(A(S))+LV(A(S)) 4klog⁡(m/δ)m+8klog⁡(m/δ)m.L_{\mathcal D}(A(S)) \le L_V(A(S)) + \sqrt{L_V(A(S)) \, \frac{4k \log(m/\delta)}{m}} + \frac{8k \log(m/\delta)}{m}.LD​(A(S))≤LV​(A(S))+LV​(A(S))m4klog(m/δ)​​+m8klog(m/δ)​.

Read it from the inside out.

  • Zk\mathcal Z^kZk is the set of sequences of kkk examples, so B:Zk→HB: \mathcal Z^k \to \mathcal HB:Zk→H says BBB turns any kkk examples into a hypothesis. For boxes, BBB draws the tightest box around the junk among its kkk examples.
  • A(S)A(S)A(S) is the hypothesis the learner returns. The theorem does not care how it chooses III; it can look at every example.
  • LV(A(S))L_V(A(S))LV​(A(S)) is the fraction of the leftover examples, the ones not at a chosen position, that the output gets wrong. This is the auditor’s exam.
  • klog⁡(m/δ)k \log(m/\delta)klog(m/δ) is the price tag. Compare it with the hold-out lemma’s log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ): the extra klog⁡mk \log mklogm pays for the union over the mkm^kmk lists.
  • Dividing by mmm and not by ∣V∣|V|∣V∣ costs a factor of 2 and makes the bound simpler; that is where m≥2km \ge 2km≥2k comes in.

In plain words: if a learner’s output can always be rebuilt from kkk of its mmm examples, its true risk is at most its error on the examples it did not keep, plus a slack of order klog⁡(m/δ)/mk \log(m/\delta)/mklog(m/δ)/m. For the auditor: k=4k = 4k=4, m=10,000m = 10{,}000m=10,000, δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05, and the leftover error is 0, so the bound is 8⋅4⋅log⁡(200,000)/10,000≈32⋅12.2/10,000≈0.0398 \cdot 4 \cdot \log(200{,}000)/10{,}000 \approx 32 \cdot 12.2/10{,}000 \approx 0.0398⋅4⋅log(200,000)/10,000≈32⋅12.2/10,000≈0.039. Had the box made 1% mistakes on the leftovers, the bound would be 0.063.

from math import log, sqrt
def bound(L_V, k, m, delta):
    c = k * log(m / delta) / m
    return L_V + sqrt(L_V * 4 * c) + 8 * c
for L_V in (0.0, 0.01):
    print(L_V, round(bound(L_V, 4, 10_000, 0.05), 4))

It prints 0.0 0.0391 and 0.01 0.063. The function bound is the right side term by term, with c standing for klog⁡(m/δ)/mk\log(m/\delta)/mklog(m/δ)/m.

Proof. For every list I∈[m]kI \in [m]^kI∈[m]k, let hI=B(SI)h_I = B(S_I)hI​=B(SI​), the hypothesis rebuilt from the examples at the positions in III, and let VIV_IVI​ be the examples at the positions not in III. Let n=m−kn = m - kn=m−k.

Step 1: one fixed list. Fix III. The hypothesis hIh_IhI​ depends only on the examples at the positions in III, and VIV_IVI​ consists of the examples at the other positions. Because the mmm examples of SSS are drawn independently, these two groups are independent, and VIV_IVI​ is a sequence of i.i.d. draws from D\mathcal DD. So the hold-out lemma applies with T=SIT = S_IT=SI​ and V=VIV = V_IV=VI​. Since III may contain repeats, ∣VI∣|V_I|∣VI​∣ can be larger than nnn, but never smaller: ∣VI∣≥m−k=n|V_I| \ge m - k = n∣VI​∣≥m−k=n. Both terms of the slack get smaller as ∣V∣|V|∣V∣ grows, so the slack computed with nnn in place of ∣VI∣|V_I|∣VI​∣ is at least as large. A larger threshold makes the bad event smaller, so the event

EI={LD(hI)−LVI(hI)≥2LVI(hI)log⁡(1/δ)n+4log⁡(1/δ)n}E_I = \left\{ L_{\mathcal D}(h_I) - L_{V_I}(h_I) \ge \sqrt{\frac{2 L_{V_I}(h_I) \log(1/\delta)}{n}} + \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{n} \right\}EI​={LD​(hI​)−LVI​​(hI​)≥n2LVI​​(hI​)log(1/δ)​​+n4log(1/δ)​}

is contained in the hold-out lemma’s bad event, and P[EI]≤δ\mathbb P[E_I] \le \deltaP[EI​]≤δ.

Step 2: all lists at once. By the union bound over the mkm^kmk lists,

P[∃I∈[m]k:EI]≤∑I∈[m]kP[EI]≤mkδ.\mathbb P\left[ \exists I \in [m]^k : E_I \right] \le \sum_{I \in [m]^k} \mathbb P[E_I] \le m^k \delta.P[∃I∈[m]k:EI​]≤I∈[m]k∑​P[EI​]≤mkδ.

Here ∃I\exists I∃I reads “there exists a list III”, and the sum runs over every list in [m]k[m]^k[m]k.

Step 3: the learner’s list is one of them. Whatever SSS is, the learner returns A(S)=hIA(S) = h_{I}A(S)=hI​ for the particular list III it chose, and then V=VIV = V_IV=VI​. If the bound fails for A(S)A(S)A(S), then EIE_IEI​ happens for that III, so “some EIE_IEI​ happens”. The learner’s choice can depend on SSS in any way at all; it cannot escape an event that covers every choice. So with probability at least 1−mkδ1 - m^k \delta1−mkδ, for the learner’s own list,

LD(A(S))≤LV(A(S))+2LV(A(S))log⁡(1/δ)n+4log⁡(1/δ)n.L_{\mathcal D}(A(S)) \le L_V(A(S)) + \sqrt{\frac{2 L_V(A(S)) \log(1/\delta)}{n}} + \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{n}.LD​(A(S))≤LV​(A(S))+n2LV​(A(S))log(1/δ)​​+n4log(1/δ)​.

Step 4: rename the confidence. Let δ′=mkδ\delta' = m^k \deltaδ′=mkδ, the failure probability we actually end up with, and assume δ′<1\delta' < 1δ′<1. Then log⁡(1/δ)=log⁡(mk/δ′)=klog⁡m+log⁡(1/δ′)\log(1/\delta) = \log(m^k / \delta') = k \log m + \log(1/\delta')log(1/δ)=log(mk/δ′)=klogm+log(1/δ′). Since k≥1k \ge 1k≥1 and log⁡(1/δ′)>0\log(1/\delta') > 0log(1/δ′)>0, we have log⁡(1/δ′)≤klog⁡(1/δ′)\log(1/\delta') \le k \log(1/\delta')log(1/δ′)≤klog(1/δ′), so

log⁡(1/δ)≤klog⁡m+klog⁡(1/δ′)=klog⁡(m/δ′).\log(1/\delta) \le k \log m + k \log(1/\delta') = k \log(m/\delta').log(1/δ)≤klogm+klog(1/δ′)=klog(m/δ′).

Step 5: from nnn to mmm. The assumption k≤m/2k \le m/2k≤m/2 gives n=m−k≥m/2n = m - k \ge m/2n=m−k≥m/2, so 1/n≤2/m1/n \le 2/m1/n≤2/m. Substituting both facts,

2LVlog⁡(1/δ)n≤LV⋅4klog⁡(m/δ′)m,4log⁡(1/δ)n≤8klog⁡(m/δ′)m.\sqrt{\frac{2 L_V \log(1/\delta)}{n}} \le \sqrt{L_V \cdot \frac{4 k \log(m/\delta')}{m}}, \qquad \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{n} \le \frac{8 k \log(m/\delta')}{m}.n2LV​log(1/δ)​​≤LV​⋅m4klog(m/δ′)​​,n4log(1/δ)​≤m8klog(m/δ′)​.

So with probability at least 1−δ′1 - \delta'1−δ′ the bound of the theorem holds with δ′\delta'δ′ in place of δ\deltaδ. Since δ′\delta'δ′ was an arbitrary number in (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1), renaming it δ\deltaδ proves the theorem. ■\blacksquare■

When the rebuilt hypothesis makes no mistake on the leftovers, the first two terms vanish, and we get the clean form that answers the auditor.

Corollary (realizable form). Under the conditions of the theorem, if also LV(A(S))=0L_V(A(S)) = 0LV​(A(S))=0, then with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ over S∼DmS \sim \mathcal D^mS∼Dm,

LD(A(S))≤8klog⁡(m/δ)m.L_{\mathcal D}(A(S)) \le \frac{8 k \log(m/\delta)}{m}.LD​(A(S))≤m8klog(m/δ)​.

In plain words: a learner whose output is rebuilt from kkk of its mmm examples and makes no mistake on the rest has true risk at most 8klog⁡(m/δ)/m8k\log(m/\delta)/m8klog(m/δ)/m. For the auditor’s box, that is the 0.039 above. For a smaller run of m=2,000m = 2{,}000m=2,000 labels it is about 0.17. How close to the truth is it? The next snippet trains the tightest box on 1,000 random training sequences of 2,000 messages each, computes each box’s exact true risk (true box area minus learned box area, as before), and compares the worst one with the bound.

import random
from math import log
rng, m, k, delta = random.Random(7), 2000, 4, 0.05
a, b = (0.3, 0.2), (0.8, 0.6)
area = lambda lo, hi: (hi[0] - lo[0]) * (hi[1] - lo[1])
risks = []
for _ in range(1000):
    xs = [(rng.random(), rng.random()) for _ in range(m)]
    P = [x for x in xs
         if all(a[j] <= x[j] <= b[j] for j in (0, 1))]
    lo = [min(x[j] for x in P) for j in (0, 1)]
    hi = [max(x[j] for x in P) for j in (0, 1)]
    risks.append(area(a, b) - area(lo, hi))
eps = 8 * k * log(m / delta) / m
print(round(eps, 4), round(max(risks), 4))
print(sum(r > eps for r in risks) / len(risks))

It prints 0.1695 0.0062 and 0.0. The bound holds every time, and it is loose: the worst of a thousand boxes had true risk 0.0062, nearly thirty times below the bound. The compression bound knows nothing about boxes except the number 4. It trades sharpness for generality, and it is the generality we came for.

Compression schemes, defined

The theorem needs a learner of the form A(S)=B(SI)A(S) = B(S_I)A(S)=B(SI​) whose rebuilt hypothesis is perfect on the leftovers. A compression scheme is the guarantee that such a learner exists for a whole class, whatever the training sequence. It has the two halves we met in the worked example: a compression function, written κ\kappaκ (the Greek letter kappa, for “keep”), that reads all mmm examples and returns kkk positions, and the reconstruction function BBB, which reads the examples at those positions and returns a hypothesis.

Recall from lesson 3 that a training sequence is realizable by H\mathcal HH when some h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H labels every example in it correctly: yi=h(xi)y_i = h(x_i)yi​=h(xi​) for all iii.

Definition (compression scheme). Let H\mathcal HH be a class of functions from X\mathcal XX to Y\mathcal YY (the set of messages and the set of labels), and kkk a positive integer. H\mathcal HH has a compression scheme of size kkk if for every mmm there are functions κ:Zm→[m]k\kappa: \mathcal Z^m \to [m]^kκ:Zm→[m]k and B:Zk→HB: \mathcal Z^k \to \mathcal HB:Zk→H such that, for every h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H and every training sequence of the form S=((x1,h(x1)),…,(xm,h(xm)))S = ((x_1, h(x_1)), \dots, (x_m, h(x_m)))S=((x1​,h(x1​)),…,(xm​,h(xm​))), if I=κ(S)I = \kappa(S)I=κ(S) then the hypothesis h′=B(SI)h' = B(S_I)h′=B(SI​) satisfies LS(h′)=0L_S(h') = 0LS​(h′)=0.

Read it piece by piece.

  • κ:Zm→[m]k\kappa: \mathcal Z^m \to [m]^kκ:Zm→[m]k turns a whole training sequence into a list of kkk positions. For boxes in two scores, it returns the positions of the four extreme junk examples.
  • B:Zk→HB: \mathcal Z^k \to \mathcal HB:Zk→H turns the kept examples into a hypothesis; for boxes, the tightest box around their junk.
  • “for every h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H and every training sequence of the form (xi,h(xi))(x_i, h(x_i))(xi​,h(xi​))” says: whatever the true hypothesis in the class is, and whatever messages arrive, as long as the labels are realizable by the class.
  • LS(h′)=0L_S(h') = 0LS​(h′)=0 says the rebuilt hypothesis is consistent with the whole sequence, the kept examples and the leftovers alike.

In plain words: a class has a compression scheme of size kkk when every realizable training sequence can be boiled down to kkk of its examples from which a hypothesis consistent with the whole sequence can be rebuilt. On the eight examples, κ\kappaκ returned (1,4,1,2)(1, 4, 1, 2)(1,4,1,2), BBB drew [0.35,0.75]×[0.25,0.5][0.35, 0.75] \times [0.25, 0.5][0.35,0.75]×[0.25,0.5], and it made 0 mistakes on all eight.

Two remarks. First, LS(h′)=0L_S(h') = 0LS​(h′)=0 means the scheme is an ERM learner in the realizable case (an empirical risk minimizer, lesson 2’s learner that returns a hypothesis with the smallest training error), and it also means LV(h′)=0L_V(h') = 0LV​(h′)=0 on the leftovers, so the corollary applies straight away: a class with a compression scheme of size kkk is learnable, with true risk at most 8klog⁡(m/δ)/m8k\log(m/\delta)/m8klog(m/δ)/m. Second, the definition is a promise about every hhh and every sequence, not about one lucky run. The snippet below tests the box scheme in three scores (k=6k = 6k=6) against 300 random true boxes, each with 500 random messages, and counts the runs where the rebuilt box makes any mistake.

import random
rng, d, failures = random.Random(16), 3, 0
for _ in range(300):
    lo = [rng.uniform(0, 0.5) for _ in range(d)]
    hi = [l + rng.uniform(0, 0.5) for l in lo]
    h = lambda x, lo, hi: int(all(a <= v <= b
                                  for v, a, b in zip(x, lo, hi)))
    xs = [[rng.random() for _ in range(d)] for _ in range(500)]
    S = [(x, h(x, lo, hi)) for x in xs]
    P = [i for i, (x, y) in enumerate(S) if y == 1] or [0]
    I = [f(P, key=lambda i: S[i][0][j]) for j in range(d)
         for f in (min, max)]
    T = [S[i][0] for i in I if S[i][1] == 1]
    lo2 = [min((x[j] for x in T), default=1) for j in range(d)]
    hi2 = [max((x[j] for x in T), default=0) for j in range(d)]
    failures += any(h(x, lo2, hi2) != y for x, y in S)
print(len(I), failures)

It prints 6 0: six positions kept, no failures. (When a sequence has no junk at all, P falls back to position 0, the kept example is a keep message, and the rebuilt “box” is empty, so it says keep everywhere, which is consistent.)

When no hypothesis is perfect

Real mail is not realizable. Users mislabel, spammers imitate keep messages, and no box gets everything right. In that agnostic setting (lesson 3’s word for “no promise that some h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H is perfect”), what should a compression scheme promise? Not zero mistakes; that may be impossible. The natural promise is: the rebuilt hypothesis does at least as well on SSS as any hypothesis in the class.

Definition (compression scheme for unrealizable sequences). H\mathcal HH has a compression scheme of size kkk for unrealizable sequences if for every mmm there are κ:Zm→[m]k\kappa: \mathcal Z^m \to [m]^kκ:Zm→[m]k and B:Zk→HB: \mathcal Z^k \to \mathcal HB:Zk→H such that for every training sequence S=((x1,y1),…,(xm,ym))S = ((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_m, y_m))S=((x1​,y1​),…,(xm​,ym​)), with any labels at all, the hypothesis h′=B(Sκ(S))h' = B(S_{\kappa(S)})h′=B(Sκ(S)​) satisfies LS(h′)≤LS(h)L_S(h') \le L_S(h)LS​(h′)≤LS​(h) for every h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H.

The only change is the last line: LS(h′)=0L_S(h') = 0LS​(h′)=0 became LS(h′)≤LS(h)L_S(h') \le L_S(h)LS​(h′)≤LS​(h) for all hhh, which says that h′h'h′ is an ERM hypothesis, one with the smallest empirical risk in the class. In plain words: every training sequence, realizable or not, can be boiled down to kkk examples from which an empirical risk minimizer can be rebuilt. For example, if the best box in the class makes 13 mistakes on SSS, the rebuilt box makes at most 13.

Do we need a new scheme for every class? No. For binary labels, a realizable scheme can be upgraded for free.

Lemma (from realizable to unrealizable). Let H\mathcal HH be a class for binary classification with a compression scheme of size kkk in the realizable case. Then it has a compression scheme of size kkk for unrealizable sequences.

Proof. Build the new compression function in three moves. Given any SSS, first find an ERM hypothesis h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H, one with LS(h)≤LS(g)L_S(h) \le L_S(g)LS​(h)≤LS​(g) for every g∈Hg \in \mathcal Hg∈H. Second, discard every example on which hhh errs; call what remains S′S'S′. Every example in S′S'S′ carries the label hhh gives it, so S′S'S′ is realizable by h∈Hh \in \mathcal Hh∈H, and the realizable scheme applies to it. Third, run the realizable compression function on S′S'S′ and translate the kkk positions it returns into positions in SSS. The reconstruction function is the realizable one, unchanged.

Now check the promise. The rebuilt hypothesis h′h'h′ is consistent with S′S'S′, so it can only err on the discarded examples, and there are exactly mLS(h)m L_S(h)mLS​(h) of those. So LS(h′)≤LS(h)≤LS(g)L_S(h') \le L_S(h) \le L_S(g)LS​(h′)≤LS​(h)≤LS​(g) for every g∈Hg \in \mathcal Hg∈H. ■\blacksquare■

The compression bound needs no change for this case: it already allows LV(A(S))>0L_V(A(S)) > 0LV​(A(S))>0. That is the agnostic form of the guarantee, and the corollary is its realizable special case.

Here is the upgrade on the simplest class there is, thresholds on one score: hθ(x)=1h_\theta(x) = 1hθ​(x)=1 when x≥θx \ge \thetax≥θ, “junk when the capitals share is at least θ\thetaθ”. Its realizable scheme has size 1: keep the junk example with the smallest score, and rebuild θ\thetaθ as that score (with no junk at all, keep any example and rebuild a θ\thetaθ above every score). The snippet draws 200 messages whose true threshold is 0.6, flips 10% of the labels, finds an ERM threshold by trying every score, discards its mistakes, keeps one example, and rebuilds.

import random
rng, m = random.Random(8), 200
xs = [rng.random() for _ in range(m)]
S = [(x, int(x >= 0.6) ^ (rng.random() < 0.1)) for x in xs]
errors = lambda th: sum(int(x >= th) != y for x, y in S)
erm = min(sorted(xs) + [2.0], key=errors)
clean = [i for i, (x, y) in enumerate(S, 1)
         if int(x >= erm) == y]
junk = [i for i in clean if S[i - 1][1] == 1]
i1 = min(junk, key=lambda i: S[i - 1][0])
th = S[i1 - 1][0]
print(errors(erm), len(clean), i1, errors(th))

It prints 13 187 186 13: the ERM threshold makes 13 mistakes, 187 examples survive the discard, the scheme keeps example 186, and the threshold rebuilt from that single example also makes 13 mistakes.

[diagram:agnostic-upgrade: built on the lesson page]

Boxes: four numbers, four examples

Now the examples. Because of the upgrade lemma, it is enough to give a realizable scheme for each class, and that is what we do.

Axis aligned rectangles in Rd\mathbb R^dRd (boxes with one interval per score, ddd scores) form an uncountably infinite class: there is a box for every choice of 2d2d2d real endpoints. Still, there is a simple scheme of size k=2dk = 2dk=2d.

  • κ\kappaκ: for each score j=1,…,dj = 1, \dots, dj=1,…,d, keep the position of a junk example with the smallest jjj-th score and one with the largest. If there is no junk example, keep any 2d2d2d positions.
  • BBB: draw the tightest box around the junk examples among the kept ones; if none of them is junk, return the hypothesis that says keep everywhere.

Why it works. If SSS has junk, the kept junk examples include an extreme in both directions for every score, so the box rebuilt from them has exactly the same 2d2d2d endpoints as the tightest box around all the junk. Lesson 8 proved that the tightest box is consistent with any realizable sequence. If SSS has no junk, every example is keep and the all-keep hypothesis is consistent. Either way LS(B(Sκ(S)))=0L_S(B(S_{\kappa(S)})) = 0LS​(B(Sκ(S)​))=0. ■\blacksquare■

That is the auditor’s four: d=2d = 2d=2 scores, k=2d=4k = 2d = 4k=2d=4.

Halfspaces: the shortest vector in the hull

The second family is the halfspaces of lesson 9. Here we switch to that lesson’s labels, y=+1y = +1y=+1 for junk and −1-1−1 for keep. A message is a vector x∈Rd\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^dx∈Rd, and a homogeneous halfspace is the hypothesis x↦sign⁡(⟨w,x⟩)\mathbf x \mapsto \operatorname{sign}(\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf x \rangle)x↦sign(⟨w,x⟩) for a weight vector w∈Rd\mathbf w \in \mathbb R^dw∈Rd, where ⟨w,x⟩=∑jwjxj\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf x \rangle = \sum_j w_j x_j⟨w,x⟩=∑j​wj​xj​ is the inner product and sign⁡\operatorname{sign}sign returns +1+1+1 for a positive number and −1-1−1 otherwise. “Homogeneous” means there is no bias term, so the boundary passes through the origin. A training sequence is realizable when some w⋆\mathbf w^\starw⋆ has yi⟨w⋆,xi⟩>0y_i \langle \mathbf w^\star, \mathbf x_i \rangle > 0yi​⟨w⋆,xi​⟩>0 for every iii. We will find a scheme of size ddd: in two dimensions, two examples are enough to rebuild a consistent halfspace, however many there are.

One trick first: fold the labels in. Since yi⟨w,xi⟩=⟨w,yixi⟩y_i \langle \mathbf w, \mathbf x_i \rangle = \langle \mathbf w, y_i \mathbf x_i \rangleyi​⟨w,xi​⟩=⟨w,yi​xi​⟩, the halfspace gets example iii right exactly when ⟨w,ui⟩>0\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle > 0⟨w,ui​⟩>0, where ui=yixi\mathbf u_i = y_i \mathbf x_iui​=yi​xi​ is the message flipped through the origin if it is keep. So we may as well pretend every label is +1+1+1 and look for a w\mathbf ww that has a positive inner product with every ui\mathbf u_iui​.

The convex hull. Recall from lesson 26: a convex combination of the points u1,…,um\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_mu1​,…,um​ is ∑iλiui\sum_i \lambda_i \mathbf u_i∑i​λi​ui​ with weights λi≥0\lambda_i \ge 0λi​≥0 that add up to 1, a weighted average. Their convex hull, written conv⁡{u1,…,um}\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf u_1, \dots, \mathbf u_m\}conv{u1​,…,um​}, is the set of all such averages: the smallest convex region containing the points, the shape a rubber band would make around them in the plane.

The scheme. κ\kappaκ finds the point w\mathbf ww of the convex hull with the smallest norm (the point of the hull closest to the origin; recall that ∥w∥=⟨w,w⟩\|\mathbf w\| = \sqrt{\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf w \rangle}∥w∥=⟨w,w⟩​ is the length of w\mathbf ww), writes it as a convex combination of at most ddd of the ui\mathbf u_iui​, and keeps their positions. BBB takes the kept examples, forms their u\mathbf uu’s, and returns the point of smallest norm in their convex hull.

Here is a small instance before the proof. Six messages in two scores, three junk and three keep:

message x\mathbf xxlabelu=yx\mathbf u = y\mathbf xu=yx
(1, 2)+1(1, 2)
(3, 1)+1(3, 1)
(2, 2)+1(2, 2)
(−1, −0.5)−1(1, 0.5)
(−2, 1)−1(2, −1)
(0.5, −2)−1(−0.5, 2)

Where would you guess the point of the hull nearest the origin lies? The candidates closest to the origin are (1,0.5)(1, 0.5)(1,0.5), at distance 1.12, and the edge from (2,−1)(2, -1)(2,−1) to (−0.5,2)(-0.5, 2)(−0.5,2), which passes even closer. The nearest point turns out to be on that edge: w=(42/61,35/61)≈(0.689,0.574)\mathbf w = (42/61, 35/61) \approx (0.689, 0.574)w=(42/61,35/61)≈(0.689,0.574), at distance 0.90. So κ\kappaκ keeps the two keep messages (−2,1)(-2, 1)(−2,1) and (0.5,−2)(0.5, -2)(0.5,−2), and BBB, seeing only those two, finds the same w\mathbf ww.

To compute a nearest point in Python we use a classic iterative method (Gilbert’s algorithm, a cousin of the Frank and Wolfe method): start at any hull point, find the data point most opposed to the current w\mathbf ww, that is, with the smallest ⟨w,u⟩\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u \rangle⟨w,u⟩, and move to the nearest point of the segment between them; repeat. Each step stays inside the hull and never increases the norm.

def dot(u, v): return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))
def min_norm(U, steps=20_000):
    w = list(U[0])
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = min(U, key=lambda u: dot(w, u))
        d = [wi - pi for wi, pi in zip(w, p)]
        if dot(d, d) == 0: break
        a = min(1.0, max(0.0, dot(w, d) / dot(d, d)))
        w = [wi - a * di for wi, di in zip(w, d)]
    return w
S = [((1, 2), 1), ((3, 1), 1), ((2, 2), 1),
     ((-1, -0.5), -1), ((-2, 1), -1), ((0.5, -2), -1)]
U = [tuple(y * xi for xi in x) for x, y in S]
w = min_norm(U)
face = [u for u in U if dot(w, u) - dot(w, w) < 1e-6]
print([round(c, 3) for c in w], face)
w2 = min_norm(face)
print([round(c, 3) for c in w2], min(dot(w2, u) for u in U) > 0)

It prints [0.689, 0.574] [(2, -1), (-0.5, 2)] and then [0.689, 0.574] True: the nearest point, the two points it rests on, the same point rebuilt from those two alone, and a check that it has a positive inner product with all six ui\mathbf u_iui​, so it labels all six messages correctly. Now let’s prove that this always works, in five steps.

[diagram:min-norm: built on the lesson page]

Step 1: the origin is not in the hull. By realizability, ⟨w⋆,ui⟩>0\langle \mathbf w^\star, \mathbf u_i \rangle > 0⟨w⋆,ui​⟩>0 for every iii. Then for any convex combination, ⟨w⋆,∑iλiui⟩=∑iλi⟨w⋆,ui⟩>0\langle \mathbf w^\star, \sum_i \lambda_i \mathbf u_i \rangle = \sum_i \lambda_i \langle \mathbf w^\star, \mathbf u_i \rangle > 0⟨w⋆,∑i​λi​ui​⟩=∑i​λi​⟨w⋆,ui​⟩>0, because the weights are non-negative and at least one is positive. The origin has inner product 0 with everything, so it is not a convex combination.

Step 2: the nearest point exists and is unique. The hull of finitely many points is closed and bounded, and the norm is continuous, so the norm attains a minimum on it; call a minimizer w\mathbf ww. By step 1, w≠0\mathbf w \ne \mathbf 0w=0. Suppose v≠w\mathbf v \ne \mathbf wv=w were another minimizer, with ∥v∥=∥w∥=r\|\mathbf v\| = \|\mathbf w\| = r∥v∥=∥w∥=r. Their midpoint is in the hull (the hull is convex), and the parallelogram identity (expand both squared norms on the right to check it) gives ∥v+w2∥2=∥v∥2+∥w∥22−∥v−w∥24<r2\left\|\frac{\mathbf v + \mathbf w}{2}\right\|^2 = \frac{\|\mathbf v\|^2 + \|\mathbf w\|^2}{2} - \frac{\|\mathbf v - \mathbf w\|^2}{4} < r^2​2v+w​​2=2∥v∥2+∥w∥2​−4∥v−w∥2​<r2, a point nearer than the nearest. So the minimizer is unique. (In fact w\mathbf ww points in the direction of the widest-margin homogeneous separator, the one lesson 15’s hard-SVM returns, but we will not need that.)

Step 3: w\mathbf ww separates the data. Suppose, for contradiction, that ⟨w,ui⟩≤0\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle \le 0⟨w,ui​⟩≤0 for some iii. Walk from w\mathbf ww a little way toward ui\mathbf u_iui​: let w′=(1−α)w+αui\mathbf w' = (1 - \alpha)\mathbf w + \alpha \mathbf u_iw′=(1−α)w+αui​ with

α=∥w∥2∥ui∥2+∥w∥2∈(0,1).\alpha = \frac{\|\mathbf w\|^2}{\|\mathbf u_i\|^2 + \|\mathbf w\|^2} \in (0, 1).α=∥ui​∥2+∥w∥2∥w∥2​∈(0,1).

(ui≠0\mathbf u_i \ne \mathbf 0ui​=0, since it is in the hull and the origin is not.) w′\mathbf w'w′ is on the segment between two hull points, so it is in the hull. Expand its squared norm:

∥w′∥2=(1−α)2∥w∥2+α2∥ui∥2+2α(1−α)⟨w,ui⟩≤(1−α)2∥w∥2+α2∥ui∥2.\|\mathbf w'\|^2 = (1-\alpha)^2 \|\mathbf w\|^2 + \alpha^2 \|\mathbf u_i\|^2 + 2\alpha(1-\alpha)\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle \le (1-\alpha)^2 \|\mathbf w\|^2 + \alpha^2 \|\mathbf u_i\|^2.∥w′∥2=(1−α)2∥w∥2+α2∥ui​∥2+2α(1−α)⟨w,ui​⟩≤(1−α)2∥w∥2+α2∥ui​∥2.

The inequality drops the cross term, which is ≤0\le 0≤0 because α(1−α)>0\alpha(1-\alpha) > 0α(1−α)>0 and ⟨w,ui⟩≤0\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle \le 0⟨w,ui​⟩≤0. Now substitute α\alphaα and 1−α=∥ui∥2/(∥ui∥2+∥w∥2)1 - \alpha = \|\mathbf u_i\|^2 / (\|\mathbf u_i\|^2 + \|\mathbf w\|^2)1−α=∥ui​∥2/(∥ui​∥2+∥w∥2):

(1−α)2∥w∥2+α2∥ui∥2=∥ui∥4∥w∥2+∥w∥4∥ui∥2(∥w∥2+∥ui∥2)2=∥ui∥2∥w∥2∥w∥2+∥ui∥2=∥w∥2⋅1∥w∥2/∥ui∥2+1<∥w∥2.(1-\alpha)^2 \|\mathbf w\|^2 + \alpha^2 \|\mathbf u_i\|^2 = \frac{\|\mathbf u_i\|^4 \|\mathbf w\|^2 + \|\mathbf w\|^4 \|\mathbf u_i\|^2}{(\|\mathbf w\|^2 + \|\mathbf u_i\|^2)^2} = \frac{\|\mathbf u_i\|^2 \|\mathbf w\|^2}{\|\mathbf w\|^2 + \|\mathbf u_i\|^2} = \|\mathbf w\|^2 \cdot \frac{1}{\|\mathbf w\|^2/\|\mathbf u_i\|^2 + 1} < \|\mathbf w\|^2.(1−α)2∥w∥2+α2∥ui​∥2=(∥w∥2+∥ui​∥2)2∥ui​∥4∥w∥2+∥w∥4∥ui​∥2​=∥w∥2+∥ui​∥2∥ui​∥2∥w∥2​=∥w∥2⋅∥w∥2/∥ui​∥2+11​<∥w∥2.

The second equality factors ∥ui∥2∥w∥2\|\mathbf u_i\|^2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥ui​∥2∥w∥2 out of the numerator and cancels one copy of the denominator; the last step holds because ∥w∥2/∥ui∥2>0\|\mathbf w\|^2 / \|\mathbf u_i\|^2 > 0∥w∥2/∥ui​∥2>0. So w′\mathbf w'w′ is a hull point strictly nearer than w\mathbf ww, a contradiction. Hence ⟨w,ui⟩>0\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle > 0⟨w,ui​⟩>0 for every iii: the nearest point of the hull is a consistent halfspace, an ERM hypothesis in the realizable case.

Step 4: w\mathbf ww rests on at most ddd points. Step 3 can be sharpened. The same walk toward any hull point p\mathbf pp shows that ⟨w,p⟩≥∥w∥2\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf p \rangle \ge \|\mathbf w\|^2⟨w,p⟩≥∥w∥2 for every p\mathbf pp in the hull. Indeed, for α∈(0,1]\alpha \in (0, 1]α∈(0,1] the point w+α(p−w)\mathbf w + \alpha(\mathbf p - \mathbf w)w+α(p−w) is in the hull, so its squared norm is at least ∥w∥2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥w∥2:

∥w∥2+2α⟨w,p−w⟩+α2∥p−w∥2≥∥w∥2.\|\mathbf w\|^2 + 2\alpha \langle \mathbf w, \mathbf p - \mathbf w \rangle + \alpha^2 \|\mathbf p - \mathbf w\|^2 \ge \|\mathbf w\|^2.∥w∥2+2α⟨w,p−w⟩+α2∥p−w∥2≥∥w∥2.

Cancel ∥w∥2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥w∥2, divide by α>0\alpha > 0α>0, and let α\alphaα shrink to 0: ⟨w,p−w⟩≥0\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf p - \mathbf w \rangle \ge 0⟨w,p−w⟩≥0, that is, ⟨w,p⟩≥∥w∥2\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf p \rangle \ge \|\mathbf w\|^2⟨w,p⟩≥∥w∥2. Call a flat any line, plane, or higher-dimensional analogue, not necessarily through the origin. In plain words: every point of the hull lies on or beyond the flat through w\mathbf ww perpendicular to w\mathbf ww, on the side away from the origin. In the example, the inner products minus ∥w∥2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥w∥2 are 1.033, 1.836, 1.721, 0.172, 0 and 0: never negative, and zero exactly on the two kept points.

from fractions import Fraction as Fr
U = [(1, 2), (3, 1), (2, 2), (1, 0.5), (2, -1), (-0.5, 2)]
w = (Fr(42, 61), Fr(35, 61))
ww = w[0] ** 2 + w[1] ** 2
gaps = [w[0] * Fr(a) + w[1] * Fr(b) - ww for a, b in U]
print([round(float(g), 3) for g in gaps])
lam = Fr(29, 61)
mix = [lam * Fr(p) + (1 - lam) * Fr(q)
       for p, q in zip(U[4], U[5])]
print(mix == list(w))

It prints [1.033, 1.836, 1.721, 0.172, 0.0, 0.0] and True, the second line confirming in exact fractions that w=2961(2,−1)+3261(−0.5,2)\mathbf w = \frac{29}{61}(2, -1) + \frac{32}{61}(-0.5, 2)w=6129​(2,−1)+6132​(−0.5,2).

Now write w=∑iλiui\mathbf w = \sum_i \lambda_i \mathbf u_iw=∑i​λi​ui​ as a convex combination. Then ∥w∥2=⟨w,w⟩=∑iλi⟨w,ui⟩\|\mathbf w\|^2 = \langle \mathbf w, \mathbf w \rangle = \sum_i \lambda_i \langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle∥w∥2=⟨w,w⟩=∑i​λi​⟨w,ui​⟩. Each ⟨w,ui⟩\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle⟨w,ui​⟩ is at least ∥w∥2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥w∥2, and the weights add up to 1, so the sum is at least ∥w∥2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥w∥2, with equality only if ⟨w,ui⟩=∥w∥2\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle = \|\mathbf w\|^2⟨w,ui​⟩=∥w∥2 for every iii with λi>0\lambda_i > 0λi​>0. Since the sum is ∥w∥2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥w∥2, equality holds. So w\mathbf ww is a convex combination of points that all lie on the flat F={p:⟨w,p⟩=∥w∥2}F = \{\mathbf p : \langle \mathbf w, \mathbf p \rangle = \|\mathbf w\|^2\}F={p:⟨w,p⟩=∥w∥2}. (In set-builder notation, the braces collect the points p\mathbf pp such that, read the colon as “such that”, their inner product with w\mathbf ww is ∥w∥2\|\mathbf w\|^2∥w∥2.) That flat is a line in the plane and, in general, a hyperplane of dimension d−1d - 1d−1. This is the precise meaning of “w\mathbf ww lies on a face of the hull”.

To get down to ddd points we need one classical fact.

Carathéodory’s theorem. If a point is a convex combination of finitely many points of a flat of dimension DDD, it is a convex combination of at most D+1D + 1D+1 of them.

The idea is easy to see in the plane, D=2D = 2D=2. The centre (1,1)(1, 1)(1,1) of the square with corners (0,0),(2,0),(0,2),(2,2)(0,0), (2,0), (0,2), (2,2)(0,0),(2,0),(0,2),(2,2) is the average of all four corners, with weights 14\frac1441​ each. But it is also the midpoint of the diagonal from (2,0)(2,0)(2,0) to (0,2)(0,2)(0,2): two points suffice, well within D+1=3D + 1 = 3D+1=3. The proof finds such a shortcut mechanically.

Proof. Let w=∑j=1qλjpj\mathbf w = \sum_{j=1}^q \lambda_j \mathbf p_jw=∑j=1q​λj​pj​ with all λj>0\lambda_j > 0λj​>0 (drop any zero weights), ∑jλj=1\sum_j \lambda_j = 1∑j​λj​=1, and q≥D+2q \ge D + 2q≥D+2. The q−1≥D+1q - 1 \ge D + 1q−1≥D+1 difference vectors p2−p1,…,pq−p1\mathbf p_2 - \mathbf p_1, \dots, \mathbf p_q - \mathbf p_1p2​−p1​,…,pq​−p1​ live in the DDD-dimensional space of directions of the flat, so they are linearly dependent: ∑j≥2cj(pj−p1)=0\sum_{j \ge 2} c_j (\mathbf p_j - \mathbf p_1) = \mathbf 0∑j≥2​cj​(pj​−p1​)=0 with the cjc_jcj​ not all zero. Set μj=cj\mu_j = c_jμj​=cj​ for j≥2j \ge 2j≥2 and μ1=−∑j≥2cj\mu_1 = -\sum_{j \ge 2} c_jμ1​=−∑j≥2​cj​. Then ∑jμjpj=0\sum_j \mu_j \mathbf p_j = \mathbf 0∑j​μj​pj​=0 and ∑jμj=0\sum_j \mu_j = 0∑j​μj​=0, and since the μj\mu_jμj​ are not all zero but add up to zero, some μj>0\mu_j > 0μj​>0. Let τ=min⁡{λj/μj:μj>0}\tau = \min\{\lambda_j / \mu_j : \mu_j > 0\}τ=min{λj​/μj​:μj​>0} and λj′=λj−τμj\lambda'_j = \lambda_j - \tau \mu_jλj′​=λj​−τμj​. Then every λj′≥0\lambda'_j \ge 0λj′​≥0 (by the choice of τ\tauτ), ∑jλj′=1−τ⋅0=1\sum_j \lambda'_j = 1 - \tau \cdot 0 = 1∑j​λj′​=1−τ⋅0=1, ∑jλj′pj=w−τ⋅0=w\sum_j \lambda'_j \mathbf p_j = \mathbf w - \tau \cdot \mathbf 0 = \mathbf w∑j​λj′​pj​=w−τ⋅0=w, and at least one λj′\lambda'_jλj′​ is 0. Drop it. Repeat until at most D+1D + 1D+1 points remain. ■\blacksquare■

Here is one step of the proof on the square. The dependence p1−p2−p3+p4=0\mathbf p_1 - \mathbf p_2 - \mathbf p_3 + \mathbf p_4 = \mathbf 0p1​−p2​−p3​+p4​=0 gives μ=(1,−1,−1,1)\mu = (1, -1, -1, 1)μ=(1,−1,−1,1), the step size is τ=14\tau = \frac14τ=41​, and two weights drop to zero at once:

from fractions import Fraction as Fr
P = [(0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 2), (2, 2)]
lam = [Fr(1, 4)] * 4
mu = [1, -1, -1, 1]
print([sum(m * p[i] for m, p in zip(mu, P)) for i in (0, 1)],
      sum(mu))
t = min(l / m for l, m in zip(lam, mu) if m > 0)
lam2 = [l - t * m for l, m in zip(lam, mu)]
w = [sum(l * p[i] for l, p in zip(lam2, P)) for i in (0, 1)]
print([str(l) for l in lam2], [str(c) for c in w])

It prints [0, 0] 0, confirming ∑jμjpj=0\sum_j \mu_j \mathbf p_j = \mathbf 0∑j​μj​pj​=0 and ∑jμj=0\sum_j \mu_j = 0∑j​μj​=0, and then ['0', '1/2', '1/2', '0'] ['1', '1']: the same point, now from two corners.

[diagram:caratheodory: built on the lesson page]

Applied to the points on the flat FFF, which has dimension D=d−1D = d - 1D=d−1, Carathéodory says w\mathbf ww is a convex combination of at most ddd of the ui\mathbf u_iui​. Those are the positions κ\kappaκ keeps. (If there are fewer than ddd, repeat one; repeating a point does not change a hull.) Applied in the whole space, D=dD = dD=d, it would give d+1d + 1d+1; the face is what saves one.

Step 5: BBB rebuilds exactly w\mathbf ww. BBB sees the kept points and returns the nearest point of their hull. That smaller hull sits inside the big one, so its nearest point is at least as far from the origin as w\mathbf ww. But w\mathbf ww itself is in the smaller hull, by step 4. So w\mathbf ww is a nearest point of the smaller hull too, and by the uniqueness of step 2 (applied to the smaller hull) it is the one. BBB returns w\mathbf ww, which by step 3 is consistent with all of SSS. ■\blacksquare■

So homogeneous halfspaces in Rd\mathbb R^dRd have a compression scheme of size ddd, and the compression bound certifies them with k=dk = dk=d.

Polynomials: halfspaces in disguise

Suppose junk is a middle band of capitals: shouting a little is suspicious, but a message that is all capitals is usually an automated alert your users want to keep. No threshold can say “junk when xxx is neither small nor large”, but a polynomial can: p(x)=c0+c1x+c2x2p(x) = c_0 + c_1 x + c_2 x^2p(x)=c0​+c1​x+c2​x2 with a negative c2c_2c2​ and two real roots is positive exactly between them, so sign⁡(p(x))\operatorname{sign}(p(x))sign(p(x)) says junk on a middle band.

Here is the observation that makes polynomials easy. Write ψ(x)=(1,x,x2)\psi(x) = (1, x, x^2)ψ(x)=(1,x,x2). Then p(x)=⟨c,ψ(x)⟩p(x) = \langle \mathbf c, \psi(x) \ranglep(x)=⟨c,ψ(x)⟩ with c=(c0,c1,c2)\mathbf c = (c_0, c_1, c_2)c=(c0​,c1​,c2​). So a degree-2 polynomial rule on one score is a homogeneous halfspace on the three numbers ψ(x)\psi(x)ψ(x). Lesson 16 used the same lift. In general, for x∈Rd\mathbf x \in \mathbb R^dx∈Rd and degree rrr, let ψ(x)\psi(\mathbf x)ψ(x) list every monomial of degree at most rrr, a product such as x1x32x_1 x_3^2x1​x32​ of at most rrr coordinates, together with the constant 1. Every polynomial of degree rrr is ⟨c,ψ(x)⟩\langle \mathbf c, \psi(\mathbf x) \rangle⟨c,ψ(x)⟩ for some vector of coefficients c\mathbf cc, so the class x↦sign⁡(p(x))\mathbf x \mapsto \operatorname{sign}(p(\mathbf x))x↦sign(p(x)) is the class of homogeneous halfspaces in the lifted space Rd′\mathbb R^{d'}Rd′, where d′d'd′ is the number of monomials:

d′=(d+rr)=O(dr) for fixed r.d' = \binom{d + r}{r} = O(d^r) \text{ for fixed } r.d′=(rd+r​)=O(dr) for fixed r.

Here (d+rr)\binom{d+r}{r}(rd+r​) (“d+rd + rd+r choose rrr”) counts the ways to choose the exponents of ddd coordinates adding up to at most rrr, and O(dr)O(d^r)O(dr) says it grows no faster than a constant times drd^rdr as ddd grows. In plain words: a degree-rrr polynomial rule in ddd scores is a halfspace in about drd^rdr lifted scores, so it has a compression scheme of that size. For one score and degree 2, d′=(32)=3d' = \binom{3}{2} = 3d′=(23​)=3, the three entries of (1,x,x2)(1, x, x^2)(1,x,x2).

from math import comb
for d, r in ((1, 2), (2, 2), (3, 2), (4, 3), (30, 2)):
    print(d, r, comb(d + r, r))

It prints 1 2 3, 2 2 6, 3 2 10, 4 3 35 and 30 2 496. Thirty scores with quadratic rules would cost a compression of size 496.

The scheme itself is the halfspace scheme, run on ui=yiψ(xi)\mathbf u_i = y_i \psi(x_i)ui​=yi​ψ(xi​): κ\kappaκ keeps at most d′d'd′ examples, and BBB lifts them, finds the nearest point of their hull, and returns the polynomial whose coefficients are that point. Eight messages, junk in the middle band of a centred capitals score:

def dot(u, v): return sum(a * b for a, b in zip(u, v))
def min_norm(U):
    w = list(U[0])
    for _ in range(100_000):
        p = min(U, key=lambda u: dot(w, u))
        d = [a - b for a, b in zip(w, p)]
        if dot(d, d) < 1e-24: break
        s = min(1.0, max(0.0, dot(w, d) / dot(d, d)))
        w = [a - s * b for a, b in zip(w, d)]
    return w
S = [(-0.93, -1), (-0.68, -1), (-0.31, 1), (0.02, 1),
     (0.13, 1), (0.22, 1), (0.57, -1), (0.97, -1)]
U = [(y, y * x, y * x * x) for x, y in S]
w = min_norm(U)
I = sorted(range(8), key=lambda i: dot(w, U[i]))[:3]
w2 = min_norm([U[i] for i in I])
print([S[i][0] for i in I], [round(c, 3) for c in w2])
print(min(dot(w2, u) for u in U) > 0)

It prints [0.22, -0.68, 0.57] [0.034, -0.016, -0.148] and True. Three messages are kept, one junk and two keep, and the polynomial rebuilt from them, p(x)=0.034−0.016x−0.148x2p(x) = 0.034 - 0.016x - 0.148x^2p(x)=0.034−0.016x−0.148x2, labels all eight correctly. Notice the kept points are the three with the smallest ⟨w,ui⟩\langle \mathbf w, \mathbf u_i \rangle⟨w,ui​⟩, the face of step 4. (Picking “the d′d'd′ smallest” is a shortcut that works here because exactly three points sit on the face. When more than d′d'd′ points sit on it, κ\kappaκ must run the Carathéodory reduction to choose among them.)

Margin: what the Perceptron remembers

The last example needs no geometry beyond lesson 9. Suppose every message has length at most 1, ∥xi∥≤1\|\mathbf x_i\| \le 1∥xi​∥≤1, and the training sequence is separated with margin γ>0\gamma > 0γ>0: some unit vector w⋆\mathbf w^\starw⋆ (one of length 1) has yi⟨w⋆,xi⟩≥γy_i \langle \mathbf w^\star, \mathbf x_i \rangle \ge \gammayi​⟨w⋆,xi​⟩≥γ for every iii, so every message sits at least γ\gammaγ from the boundary on its correct side. Lesson 9 proved that the Perceptron then stops after at most (R/γ)2(R/\gamma)^2(R/γ)2 updates, where RRR is the largest message length; here R≤1R \le 1R≤1, so at most 1/γ21/\gamma^21/γ2.

Now look at what the Perceptron’s final weight vector is. It starts at 0\mathbf 00, and each update adds yixiy_i \mathbf x_iyi​xi​ for the example it got wrong. So the output is

w=∑t=1Tyitxit,\mathbf w = \sum_{t=1}^{T} y_{i_t} \mathbf x_{i_t},w=t=1∑T​yit​​xit​​,

where TTT is the number of updates and iti_tit​ is the position of the example used in update ttt. In plain words: the Perceptron’s answer is the sum of the examples it stumbled on, each pointed along its label. That is a compression scheme. κ\kappaκ runs the Perceptron and keeps the list of update positions (i1,…,iT)(i_1, \dots, i_T)(i1​,…,iT​), with repeats, since the Perceptron may stumble on the same example several times. BBB adds up yxy \mathbf xyx over the kept examples, which reproduces the Perceptron’s final w\mathbf ww exactly, and that vector makes no mistake on SSS because the Perceptron only stops when nothing is wrong. The size is T≤1/γ2T \le 1/\gamma^2T≤1/γ2. This is where repeats in [m]k[m]^k[m]k earn their keep: a list of update positions is naturally a list with repeats.

import math, random
rng, gamma, u = random.Random(2), 0.1, (math.cos(1), math.sin(1))
dot = lambda w, x: w[0] * x[0] + w[1] * x[1]
S = []
while len(S) < 200:
    x = (rng.uniform(-1, 1), rng.uniform(-1, 1))
    if math.hypot(*x) <= 1 and gamma <= abs(dot(u, x)) <= 0.2:
        S.append((x, 1 if dot(u, x) > 0 else -1))
w, I = [0.0, 0.0], []
while (i := next((i for i, (x, y) in enumerate(S, 1)
                  if y * dot(w, x) <= 0), None)):
    (x, y) = S[i - 1]
    w, I = [w[0] + y * x[0], w[1] + y * x[1]], I + [i]
v = [sum(S[i - 1][1] * S[i - 1][0][j] for i in I) for j in (0, 1)]
print(len(I), round(1 / gamma ** 2), len(set(I)))
print(sum(y * dot(v, x) <= 0 for x, y in S))

It prints 21 100 5 and 0: 200 messages squeezed into a band just outside margin 0.1, a Perceptron run of 21 updates (the bound allows 100) that used only 5 distinct messages, and a replayed vector v\mathbf vv with no mistakes.

One technical wrinkle. The theorem was stated for a scheme of exactly kkk positions, but the Perceptron’s list has at most 1/γ21/\gamma^21/γ2 entries, and padding it would change the sum. The fix is to let the union bound in the proof run over all lists of every length j=1,…,kj = 1, \dots, kj=1,…,k, and give BBB the length. There are ∑j=1kmj≤2mk\sum_{j=1}^k m^j \le 2m^k∑j=1k​mj≤2mk such lists when m≥2m \ge 2m≥2 (a geometric sum whose terms at least double each time), and each still leaves at least m−km - km−k examples, so the same proof goes through with δ′=2mkδ\delta' = 2m^k\deltaδ′=2mkδ. That changes log⁡(m/δ)\log(m/\delta)log(m/δ) into log⁡(2m/δ)\log(2m/\delta)log(2m/δ) in the final bound, and nothing else.
