The algorithms

Two schemes are worth writing down as code, because they are what the lab runs and what you will build: the box scheme and the Perceptron scheme. Here SSS has mmm examples with ddd scores each.

CompressBox(S):
  P ← positions i with y_i = 1
  if P is empty: return (1, 1, ..., 1)        (2d entries)
  I ← empty list
  for j = 1..d:
    append to I a position in P with the smallest x_{i,j}
    append to I a position in P with the largest x_{i,j}
  return I

RebuildBox(T):                                 (T = k examples)
  Q ← messages x in T with label 1
  if Q is empty: return the all-keep hypothesis
  for j = 1..d:
    a_j ← min of x_j over Q;  b_j ← max of x_j over Q
  return h(x) = 1 if a_j ≤ x_j ≤ b_j for all j, else 0

CompressPerceptron(S):
  w ← 0;  I ← empty list
  while some i has y_i ⟨w, x_i⟩ ≤ 0:
    w ← w + y_i x_i;  append i to I
  return I

Replay(T):
  return the halfspace of w = sum of y x over (x, y) in T

CompressBox makes one pass per score over the junk examples: O(md)O(md)O(md) time, O(d)O(d)O(d) space for the 2d2d2d positions beyond the input. RebuildBox reads 2d2d2d examples of ddd scores: O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2) time. The compressed certificate, 2d2d2d messages, does not grow with mmm at all, which is the whole point. CompressPerceptron is lesson 9’s Perceptron with a notebook: O(md/γ2)O(m d / \gamma^2)O(md/γ2) time on separable data with margin γ\gammaγ and radius 1, since each of at most 1/γ21/\gamma^21/γ2 updates follows a scan of O(md)O(md)O(md), and O(d+1/γ2)O(d + 1/\gamma^2)O(d+1/γ2) space. Replay costs O(d/γ2)O(d/\gamma^2)O(d/γ2).

The halfspace scheme is costlier. Finding the nearest point of a hull is a convex quadratic program; Gilbert’s method above approaches it step by step, with each step costing O(md)O(md)O(md). The Carathéodory reduction then removes one point per round, at most mmm rounds, each a Gaussian elimination on d+1d + 1d+1 points of the face, O(d3)O(d^3)O(d3), so O(md3)O(md^3)O(md3) in all. The reconstruction solves the same problem on ddd points only.

Build it yourself. Using only the standard library:

from math import log

S = [((0.35, 0.25), 1), ((0.6, 0.5), 1), ((0.5, 0.3), 1),
     ((0.75, 0.4), 1), ((0.1, 0.3), 0), ((0.9, 0.5), 0),
     ((0.5, 0.8), 0), ((0.4, 0.1), 0)]
S3 = [((0.4, 0.5, 0.2), 1), ((0.7, 0.3, 0.6), 1),
      ((0.5, 0.45, 0.4), 1), ((0.2, 0.4, 0.3), 0),
      ((0.6, 0.9, 0.5), 0), ((0.55, 0.4, 0.95), 0)]

def compress_box(S, d): ...
def reconstruct_box(T): ...
def predict(box, x): ...
def certified_risk(k, m, delta): ...
def min_labels(k, eps, delta): ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    I = compress_box(S, 2)
    assert I == [1, 4, 1, 2]
    box = reconstruct_box([S[i - 1] for i in I])
    assert box == [(0.35, 0.75), (0.25, 0.5)]
    assert all(predict(box, x) == y for x, y in S)
    I3 = compress_box(S3, 3)
    box3 = reconstruct_box([S3[i - 1] for i in I3])
    assert len(I3) == 6
    assert all(predict(box3, x) == y for x, y in S3)
    assert compress_box([((0.1, 0.1), 0)], 2) == [1, 1, 1, 1]
    empty = reconstruct_box([((0.1, 0.1), 0)] * 4)
    assert predict(empty, (0.1, 0.1)) == 0
    assert round(certified_risk(4, 10_000, 0.05), 4) == 0.0391
    assert min_labels(4, 0.05, 0.05) == 7640
    assert min_labels(6, 0.05, 0.05) == 11884
  1. Implement the five functions. Positions are 1-based; compress_box returns 2d2d2d of them, smallest then largest for each score, ties broken by the first position; reconstruct_box returns a list of ddd intervals, or None for the all-keep hypothesis; certified_risk is the realizable bound 8klog⁡(m/δ)/m8k\log(m/\delta)/m8klog(m/δ)/m; min_labels is the smallest m≥2km \ge 2km≥2k whose certified risk is at most ε\varepsilonε.
  2. Add compress_perceptron(S) and replay(T) for ±1\pm 1±1 labels, and check on random data with margin 0.1 that the list has at most 100 entries and the replay makes no mistake.
  3. Re-run the auditor’s experiment from the opening with compress_box, then delete one unkept message and one kept message in turn. Which deletion can change the box?

Fix the bug

The auditor’s report is back, and it has a request in it. Next quarter the filter gets a third score, x3x_3x3​, the share of misspelled words in the subject, so it will draw boxes in three scores. Compliance wants a written certificate before training: with probability at least 95% (δ=0.05\delta = 0.05δ=0.05), the filter’s true risk will be at most 5% (ε=0.05\varepsilon = 0.05ε=0.05). Labels cost money, and the budget is 12,000.

You now have the tool. A certificate needs two things, and the lab checks both. First, a compression scheme for boxes in three scores: a compression function and a reconstruction function whose rebuilt box makes no mistake on the whole training sequence, so that the corollary applies. Second, a number of labels mmm for which 8klog⁡(m/δ)/m≤0.058k\log(m/\delta)/m \le 0.058klog(m/δ)/m≤0.05, with kkk the size of your scheme. The smaller your kkk, the fewer labels you need. Before you open the lab, work out what each kkk costs:

from math import log
def min_labels(k, eps, delta):
    m = 2 * k
    while 8 * k * log(m / delta) / m > eps:
        m += 1
    return m
print([min_labels(k, 0.05, 0.05) for k in (4, 6, 8, 12)])

It prints [7640, 11884, 16245, 25212]. A scheme of size 4 would fit the budget easily, but can four examples always pin down a box in three scores? A cautious scheme that keeps two examples per end of each interval has size 12 and needs 25,212 labels. Somewhere in between is the smallest size your scheme can guarantee, and only that one fits.

[lab-act2: built on the lesson page]

What people get wrong

“The leftover examples are a fresh test set, so their error estimates the true risk directly.” They are not fresh: the kept examples were chosen after looking at all of them. The hold-out lemma applies to every fixed list of positions, and the union over all mkm^kmk lists is what makes it apply to the learner’s chosen one. That union costs klog⁡mk\log mklogm, which is why the bound has klog⁡(m/δ)k\log(m/\delta)klog(m/δ) where a true hold-out would have log⁡(1/δ)\log(1/\delta)log(1/δ).

“The size of the scheme is the number of different examples it keeps.” The size is the length kkk of the list the compression function returns, fixed for the class in advance. On the eight examples the box scheme kept three different messages in four slots, and the bound still uses k=4k = 4k=4. The theorem’s union runs over all lists of length kkk, and that count, mkm^kmk, is what the size measures.

“A small certified risk means the bound is close to the truth.” The bound only uses kkk. On 2,000 labels it certified 0.17 while the worst of a thousand real boxes had true risk 0.006. The certificate is a guarantee, not a forecast; its strength is that it needs nothing but the size of the scheme.

“Any class with a compression scheme in the realizable case needs a new scheme for noisy data.” For binary labels the upgrade is free: find an ERM hypothesis, discard its mistakes, compress what is left. The bound then compares the true risk with the leftover error, which is no longer zero.

Where this sits

Look at what this lesson added to the list of reasons a learner generalizes. Lesson 4 said: when every hypothesis’s training error tracks its true error at once (uniform convergence). Lesson 13 said: when the learner barely changes if one example changes (stability). Today: when the learner’s output can be described by a few of its own examples. It is the most “engineering” of the three, because it is a fact about the learner’s output that you can check by deleting data and retraining, exactly as the auditor did.

The three are connected. A class of binary hypotheses with a compression scheme of size kkk is learnable, as the corollary shows, so by the fundamental theorem of lesson 6 its VC dimension is finite. The converse is a deeper question: does every class of finite VC dimension have a compression scheme of finite size? Manfred Warmuth posed it as an open problem. A later result by Moran and Yehudayoff showed that the answer is yes, with a size that may grow exponentially in the VC dimension; whether a size of the order of the VC dimension always suffices is still being studied.

Recap and the next bug

  1. A compression scheme of size kkk is a pair of functions: κ\kappaκ chooses kkk positions from the training sequence (repeats allowed), and BBB rebuilds a hypothesis from the examples at those positions, consistent with the whole sequence in the realizable case and an ERM in the unrealizable case.
  2. Bernstein’s inequality bounds a sum of bounded, mean-zero quantities using their variance. For a fixed hypothesis it gives LD(h)≤LS(h)+2LS(h)log⁡(1/δ)/m+4log⁡(1/δ)/mL_{\mathcal D}(h) \le L_S(h) + \sqrt{2L_S(h)\log(1/\delta)/m} + 4\log(1/\delta)/mLD​(h)≤LS​(h)+2LS​(h)log(1/δ)/m​+4log(1/δ)/m with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ: a slack of order 1/m1/m1/m when the error is small.
  3. A hypothesis built from some examples and graded on others it never saw obeys that bound on the others. When the kept examples are chosen by looking, a union bound over all mkm^kmk lists pays klog⁡mk \log mklogm, giving the compression bound LD≤LV+LV⋅4klog⁡(m/δ)/m+8klog⁡(m/δ)/mL_{\mathcal D} \le L_V + \sqrt{L_V \cdot 4k\log(m/\delta)/m} + 8k\log(m/\delta)/mLD​≤LV​+LV​⋅4klog(m/δ)/m​+8klog(m/δ)/m, and 8klog⁡(m/δ)/m8k\log(m/\delta)/m8klog(m/δ)/m when the leftovers are all correct.
  4. A realizable scheme for binary labels upgrades to an unrealizable one of the same size: ERM, discard its mistakes, compress the rest.
  5. Boxes in ddd scores compress to 2d2d2d examples; homogeneous halfspaces in Rd\mathbb R^dRd to ddd, via the nearest point of the hull and Carathéodory on its face; degree-rrr polynomial rules to (d+rr)=O(dr)\binom{d+r}{r} = O(d^r)(rd+r​)=O(dr), by lifting to monomials; and data separated with margin γ\gammaγ to the at most 1/γ21/\gamma^21/γ2 updates of the Perceptron.

The certificate is signed, and the auditor is satisfied. Then your own team comes back with a request of a different kind. Over the years you have all come to trust some rules more than others before seeing any mail at all: narrow boxes around last year’s campaign, halfspaces that lean on the link score. And instead of shipping one rule, they want to ship a weighted mix: pick a rule at random from a distribution you believe in, and let it decide each message. Every bound so far, VC, Rademacher, stability, compression, treats the learner’s output as one rule. What does a guarantee for a whole weighted mix of rules look like, and how does a prior belief over rules, held before any data arrives, turn into one? That is the next lesson.
